#### What type of PR is this?

<!--
Add one of the following kinds:
/kind bug

Optionally add one or more of the following kinds if applicable:
/kind api-change

/kind flake
/kind regression
-->

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

This PR locks the `ExecProbeTimeout` feature-gate to true so that it is always enabled. Practically speaking, this means that "exec probe timeouts always actually work".

The background for providing a feature-gate to "break" exec probe timeout functionality is the following:

- exec probe timeouts were non-functional for all Kubernetes releases until 1.20
- the sudden introduction of functional exec probe timeouts, when combined with a default timeout value of 1 second, meant that some Kubernetes users would receive an undesirable change (enforcement of a 1 second timeout) in their workload definitions when upgrading to 1.20
- for such users, a convenient `-feature-gates=ExecProbeTimeout=false` configuration was provided so that the pre-1.20.0 behavior would be preserved

All of the above background is true _for dockershim only_. For non-dockershim CRI (e.g., containerd), the pre-1.20.0 behavior was actually much worse than "exec probe timeouts are not enforced": for these non-dockershim scenarios, in pre-1.20.0 releases of Kubernetes, any probe whose time duration exceeds this new default timeout value (1 second) will *always suceed*. In other words, if a probe command returns non-zero, but if that probe's runtime duration takes longer than 1 second, then that probe will actually not fail and restart the underlying container as intended. This nasty behavior persists in Kubernetes @ HEAD, where dockershim has been permanently removed. And thus there is no recommended scenario in which we want to continue providing folks with this broken exec probe behavior.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:

Usage: `Fixes #<issue number>`, or `Fixes (paste link of issue)`.

-->
Fixes #99854

> But for non-dockershim, the pre-1.20 behavior was pathological (see the above example) and so we don't actually want to preserve it. 

The problem is always that this change will break customers. If probe results in always succeeding, changing the behavior to something that will start failing is a breaking change that we want to avoid.

I think in order to lock the feature gate we should give customers way to understand what value to configure the timeout value to. Thus we need that duration metric.

There are too many workloads using exec timeouts. Many for gRPC calls. So introducing built-in gRPC probes will also help with customers migration without breaking the workload unexpectedly.

I'd suggest to wait with locking of this feature

> /hold
> 
> > But for non-dockershim, the pre-1.20 behavior was pathological (see the above example) and so we don't actually want to preserve it.
> 
> The problem is always that this change will break customers. If probe results in always succeeding, changing the behavior to something that will start failing is a breaking change that we want to avoid.
> 
> I think in order to lock the feature gate we should give customers way to understand what value to configure the timeout value to. Thus we need that duration metric.
> 
> There are too many workloads using exec timeouts. Many for gRPC calls. So introducing built-in gRPC probes will also help with customers migration without breaking the workload unexpectedly.
> 
> I'd suggest to wait with locking of this feature

I understand this point of view in theory, but in this case by preserving this pre-1.20 non-dockershim behaviors we are continuing to allow customers to run probe commands that don't actually do what they say they do. I think we can confidently predict that no customer wants a failed probe command to return success. It's *possible* that there are customers running a very specific version of a buggy probe implementation itself:

- always takes longer than 1 second
- always fails

*And* that customer is explicitly opting to preserve the pre-1.20 behavior by manually configuring kubelets to `-feature-gates=ExecProbeTimeout=false`. For this customer the impact of removing the ExecProbeTimeout=false configuration will mean that they are finally required to fix their buggy probes as a result of seeing those pods finally fail.

This customer persona is theoretically possible, but I would predict it's more likely than not that this customer doesn't exist in reality.

Happy to help by reinforcing our guidance so that the communication around this is better, but we want to be clear that by delaying this we are choosing to prioritize enabling that hypothetical customer scenario and to not prioritize making sure that no 1.24 customers have non-deterministic probe behaviors.

issue_context.title: Definitive end date for ExecProbeTimeout kubelet feature gate
issue_context.body:
<!-- Feature requests are unlikely to make progress as an issue.

Instead, please suggest enhancements by engaging with SIGs on slack and mailing lists.

A proposal that works through the design along with the implications of the change can be opened as a KEP:
https://git.k8s.io/enhancements/keps#kubernetes-enhancement-proposals-keps
-->

#### What would you like to be added:

The `ExecProbeTimeout` feature gate was introduced with this bug fix:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/94115

Because the above bug fix had a practical side-effect of introducing new, 1 second exec livenessProbe timeout enforcement for all container specs not otherwise declaring a timeout, the feature gate was provided as a way to optionally opt out of that new timeout enforcment, retaining the old (buggy) behavior.

With the arrival of that feature gate was the understanding that it should be quickly locked and removed in the very next release cycle (it landed prior to the shipment of 1.20.0, and would be locked to true [essentially not usable] in the 1.21.0 release).

#### Why is this needed:

This issue advocates that the Kubernetes user community needs more time to understand the impact of the 1 second default timeout side-effect, and hence to allow folks to continue to opt out of this change if that side-effect has undesirable costs for production workloads running in their environments.

The deliverable for this issue should be a more permissive, final decision on when to disable usage of the `ExecProbeTimeout` feature gate, which would yield two practical work tasks:

1. Update the code comment here with the decision:
  - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.20.0/pkg/features/kube_features.go#L826
2. Add that decision in the relevant changelog release notes so that it is easier for Kubernetes users to discover how long they may continue to use this feature gate if they wish. Refer to this original comment in the 1.20.0 changelog:
  - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.20.0/CHANGELOG/CHANGELOG-1.20.md#no-really-you-must-read-this-before-you-upgrade

Specifically, the current official messaging is:

> This gate will be locked and removed in future releases so that exec probe timeouts are always respected.

Let's pick a definitive EOL for this feature gate and publish the decision.

review_comments:
No objections locking this gate, but I personally don't see a lot of harm is keeping it unlocked for longer either. The amount of code required on our end to maintain this is very small and manageable IMO. 

Waiting 4 releases actually seems pretty reasonable to lock this, but just curious if there's a particular reason for locking it now instead of waiting a little longer, are we confident that most folks have made the appropriate fixes?

Good question. It's because the `ExecProbeTimeout=false` configuration doesn't actually work for non-dockershim (of course there is no other CRI abstraction going forward. Specifically, this scenario will engage an edge case bug that yields a liveness probe result of always success:

```
    args:
    - /bin/sh
    - -c
    - while true; do rm -f /tmp/healthy; sleep 5; done
    livenessProbe:
      exec:
        command: ['sh', '-c', 'sleep 5 && test -f /tmp/healthy']
      initialDelaySeconds: 1
      periodSeconds: 1
      failureThreshold: 1
      timeoutSeconds: 1
```

I've tried to describe this in the PR description as well. tl;dr the `ExecProbeTimeout=false` "preserve the pre-1.20 behavior" solution made sense for dockershim, because it simply disabled exec probe timeout enforcement while preserving the integrity of the probe response itself (this is what the pre-1.20 behavior was, in summary). But for non-dockershim, the pre-1.20 behavior was pathological (see the above example) and so we don't actually want to preserve it. Rather, we want to force folks onto this 1.20+ happy path, because otherwise their exec probe enforcement is actually buggy (any probe that takes longer than 1 second by default will alwyas succeed, regardless of whether or not the probe command returns a non-zero exit code).

> Rather, we want to force folks onto this 1.20+ happy path, because otherwise their exec probe enforcement is actually buggy (any probe that takes longer than 1 second by default will alwyas succeed, regardless of whether or not the probe command returns a non-zero exit code).

Aren't we already doing this by having the feature gate on by default? Or are there non-dockershim users that are incorrectly turning it off thinking they want to perserve the old behavior?

I'm not sure that those non-dockershim users are aware that this feature-gate isn't designed for them, as this pathology was only discovered after the 1.20 release landed and the general guidance about why you might want to use it was issued (that guidance AFAIK did not emphasize _For dockershim Scenarios Only!_).
